data.prompt: Which of these is made of atoms?

options.label: The light from a lamp
options.note: Light is energy, not matter.

options.label: A shadow
options.note: A shadow is just a place where light is blocked.

options.label: A sound
options.note: Sound is a wave moving through matter. It is not matter itself.

data.explanation: Air is matter, so it is made of atoms. Light, shadows and sounds are not matter.

data.prompt: A pumped-up ball weighs more than a flat one because air is made of ___.
data.explanation: Air is matter, and atoms have weight. More air inside the ball means more atoms, so it weighs more.

data.prompt: Put these in order from smallest to biggest.
data.explanation: An atom is the smallest. A virus is bigger, a skin cell is bigger still, and a hand is the biggest.

data.prompt: Which of these are made of atoms? Sort each one.
data.explanation: Phones and apples are matter, and all matter is made of atoms. Light and heat are energy, not matter.

data.statement: A bottle with only air in it is empty.
data.explanation: Myth. Air is matter, so the bottle is full of atoms. Only a vacuum, where the air has been pumped out, comes close to empty.

data.statement: Atoms are too small to be seen with an ordinary microscope.
data.explanation: True. An ordinary microscope uses light, and light waves are too big to show something as small as an atom. Special instruments can, but a classroom microscope cannot.

data.statement: With a good ordinary microscope you can see a single atom.
data.explanation: Myth. Atoms are far too small. Even the best ordinary microscope cannot show one.

data.prompt: Where is almost all of an atom's mass?

options.label: In the electrons
options.note: Electrons are very light. Almost all of the mass is in the nucleus.

options.label: Spread evenly through the atom
options.note: The mass is not spread out. It is packed into the nucleus.

data.explanation: Almost all of an atom's mass is packed into its tiny nucleus.

data.prompt: Tap the nucleus of the atom.
data.explanation: The nucleus is the tiny centre of the atom. Protons and neutrons are in it. The electrons are outside.

data.prompt: Match each particle to its charge.
data.explanation: Protons are positive, neutrons have no charge and electrons are negative.

data.prompt: Imagine an atom blown up to the size of a football stadium. How big would its nucleus be?
data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. The answer comes later in the lesson.

data.prompt: Where is each particle? Sort them.
data.explanation: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus. Electrons are outside it.

data.statement: An atom is a solid ball, packed full of stuff.
data.explanation: Myth. An atom is mostly empty space. The nucleus is a tiny speck in the middle, and the electrons are far from it.

data.statement: The nucleus takes up most of the space in an atom.
data.explanation: Myth. The nucleus is a tiny speck at the centre. Most of the atom is empty space around it.

data.prompt: A carbon atom gains 2 protons. What is it now?

options.label: Still carbon
options.note: Carbon has 6 protons. With 8 it is a different element.

options.label: Nitrogen
options.note: Nitrogen has 7 protons. That is only one more.

data.explanation: 6 protons plus 2 is 8 protons, and 8 protons is oxygen.

data.prompt: What makes an atom of gold different from an atom of oxygen?

options.label: They have different numbers of protons
They are made of different kinds of stuff
options.note: Every atom is built from the same three particles. Only the numbers are different.

options.label: Gold atoms are solid and oxygen atoms are hollow
options.note: Atoms of every element are mostly empty space.

data.explanation: Gold atoms have 79 protons and oxygen atoms have 8. The particles are the same kinds. The number of protons is what is different.

data.prompt: An oxygen atom has 8 protons. It loses one proton. What is it now?

options.label: Still oxygen
options.note: Oxygen has 8 protons. With 7, the atom is a different element.

options.label: Carbon
options.note: Carbon has 6 protons. That would mean losing two.

data.explanation: 8 protons take away 1 is 7 protons, and 7 protons is nitrogen.

data.prompt: An atom with 6 protons is always ___.
data.explanation: 6 protons is always carbon. 7 is always nitrogen, and 8 is always oxygen.

data.prompt: What is the real difference between an atom of gold and an atom of oxygen?

options.label: They have different numbers of protons
They are made of different kinds of stuff
Gold atoms are solid balls and oxygen atoms are hollow

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. Find out as you build.

data.statement: A carbon atom that gains one proton is still carbon.
data.explanation: Myth. Carbon has 6 protons. With one more it has 7, and 7 protons is nitrogen. Change the protons and you change the element.

data.prompt: Atom X has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Atom Y has 17 protons and 20 neutrons. What are X and Y?

options.label: Two different elements
options.note: They have the same number of protons, so they are the same element.

options.label: Exactly the same kind of atom
options.note: Their neutrons are different, so they are different isotopes.

data.explanation: Same protons (17) means the same element. Different neutrons (18 and 20) mean different isotopes.

data.prompt: What do isotopes of the same element share?

options.label: The same number of neutrons
options.note: Different neutrons are exactly what makes them different isotopes.

options.label: Nothing: they are different elements
options.note: Isotopes of one element are the same element.

data.explanation: Isotopes of an element all have the same number of protons, which is why they are the same element. They have different numbers of neutrons.

data.prompt: Two atoms are both carbon. Can one be heavier than the other?

options.label: Yes, they can have different weights
No, all carbon atoms are identical

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. Build a heavier carbon atom in the next card.

data.prompt: Carbon always has 6 protons. Which of these atoms are carbon? Sort each one.
data.explanation: Only the protons decide the element. Any atom with 6 protons is carbon, whatever its neutrons. The two carbon atoms with different neutrons are isotopes of carbon.

data.prompt: Each card shows two atoms. Are they isotopes of one element, or different elements?
data.explanation: Check the protons first. Same protons means the same element, so different neutrons make isotopes. Different protons means different elements.

data.statement: All isotopes are radioactive.
data.explanation: Myth. Isotope just means a version of an element. Most of the atoms around you are stable isotopes. Only some isotopes are radioactive.

data.statement: Carbon-13 is an isotope of carbon, and it is not radioactive.
data.explanation: True. Carbon-13 is a stable isotope. Being an isotope does not make an atom radioactive.

data.prompt: An atom has an unstable nucleus. What can happen to it?

options.label: The nucleus can change and give off radiation
Nothing: it stays exactly as it is for ever
options.note: Unstable means it can change.

options.label: The whole atom disappears
options.note: The nucleus changes into a different nucleus. Nothing vanishes.

data.explanation: An unstable nucleus can change and give off radiation. That is radioactivity.

data.prompt: Does every atom stay exactly the same for ever?

options.label: Yes, every atom stays the same

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. Find out in the next cards.

data.prompt: Where do these radioactive atoms come from? Sort each one.

items.label: Carbon-14 made high in the air
An isotope made in a reactor for a hospital

data.explanation: People can make radioactive atoms, but most radioactivity around us is natural: in rocks, in the air, in food and even in you.

data.prompt: Which of these atoms are stable? Sort each one.
data.explanation: Carbon-12 and oxygen-16 are stable. Carbon-14 and uranium-238 are unstable, which means radioactive.

data.statement: Every atom stays the same for ever.
data.explanation: Myth. Most atoms around us do stay the same, but an unstable nucleus can change.

data.statement: Most of the atoms in your body are stable.
data.explanation: True. Almost all of your atoms are stable. A tiny number are naturally unstable, such as potassium-40.

data.statement: Radioactive atoms only exist because people made them.
data.explanation: Myth. Radioactive atoms occur in nature. Potassium-40 is in bananas and in your own body, and carbon-14 is made high in the air.

data.prompt: You pump air into a flat ball and it gets heavier. What does that tell you?

options.label: Air is matter, so it has weight
Air is nothing, so the ball only looks heavier
options.note: If air were nothing, adding it could not change the weight.

options.label: Air is energy, not matter
options.note: Energy such as light and heat is not made of atoms. Air is.

data.explanation: The ball gets heavier because air is made of atoms, and atoms have weight.

data.statement: The electrons of an atom are packed inside the nucleus.
data.explanation: Myth. The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons. Electrons are outside it.

data.prompt: If you could shrink down and look inside an atom, what would you mostly see?

options.label: Solid stuff packed tightly
options.note: An atom is mostly empty space.

options.label: A crowd of electrons
options.note: An atom has only a few electrons, and they are far apart.

data.explanation: Most of an atom is empty space. The nucleus is a tiny speck, and the electrons are far from it.

data.statement: Isotopes of one element have different numbers of neutrons.
data.explanation: True. That is what makes them different isotopes of the same element.

data.prompt: Which statement about isotopes is true?

options.label: Some are stable and some are radioactive
All of them are radioactive
options.note: Most of the atoms around you are stable isotopes.

options.label: None of them are radioactive
options.note: Some isotopes, such as carbon-14, are radioactive.

data.explanation: Isotopes can be stable or radioactive. Carbon-12 is stable and carbon-14 is radioactive.

data.statement: Carbon-12 is an isotope, and it is stable.
data.explanation: True. Carbon-12 is a stable isotope of carbon.

data.prompt: What are carbon-12 and carbon-14?

options.label: Two different elements
options.note: Both have 6 protons, so both are carbon.

data.explanation: They are isotopes of carbon: the same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons.

data.prompt: Which particle has a negative electric charge?

options.label: The proton
options.note: Protons are positive.

options.label: The neutron
options.note: Neutrons have no charge.

data.explanation: Electrons are negative. Protons are positive and neutrons have no charge.

data.statement: Neutrons have no electric charge.
data.explanation: True. That is why they are called neutrons.

data.prompt: Which of these is NOT made of atoms?

options.label: The wood in a campfire
options.note: Wood is matter, so it is made of atoms.

options.label: The air around the fire
options.note: Air is matter, so it is made of atoms.

options.label: The ash left behind
options.note: Ash is matter, so it is made of atoms.

options.label: The heat you feel from the fire

data.explanation: Heat is energy, not matter, so it is not made of atoms. The wood, the air and the ash are all matter.

data.prompt: Compared with the whole atom, how big is the nucleus?

options.label: Tiny: a speck at the centre
About half the width of the atom
options.note: The nucleus is much, much smaller than that.

options.label: About the same size as the atom
options.note: The atom is far bigger than its nucleus.

data.explanation: The nucleus is a tiny speck at the centre of the atom.

data.prompt: Which of these is the smallest?

options.label: A virus
options.note: A virus is much bigger than an atom.

options.label: A skin cell
options.note: A skin cell is far bigger than an atom.

options.label: A hand
options.note: A hand is the biggest of these.

data.explanation: An atom is far smaller than a virus, a cell or a hand.

data.prompt: How many protons does every oxygen atom have?

options.note: 6 protons would make it carbon.
7 protons would make it nitrogen.

data.explanation: Every oxygen atom has 8 protons.

data.statement: A banana contains a tiny amount of natural radioactive potassium.
data.explanation: True. A small share of the potassium in a banana is potassium-40, which is radioactive.

data.prompt: A nitrogen atom has 7 protons. It gains one proton. What happens?

options.label: It becomes oxygen, a different element
It is still nitrogen, just heavier
options.note: The protons decide the element, so adding one changes the element.

options.label: It becomes carbon
options.note: Carbon has fewer protons, not more.

data.explanation: 7 protons plus 1 is 8 protons, and 8 protons is oxygen.

data.prompt: A rock from the ground gives off a little radiation. How can that be?

options.label: Some atoms in it are naturally unstable
Someone must have made it radioactive
options.note: Radioactivity is natural. Many rocks contain unstable atoms.

data.explanation: Some atoms in the rock, such as uranium, are naturally unstable, so it gives off a little radiation.

data.statement: Two atoms with different numbers of protons can be the same element.
data.explanation: Myth. The number of protons tells you the element. Different numbers of protons mean different elements.

data.prompt: Why can't you see atoms with an ordinary microscope?

options.label: There are not enough of them
options.note: There are enormous numbers of atoms in everything.

options.label: They are made of energy
options.note: Atoms are matter, not energy.

data.explanation: Atoms are far too small for an ordinary microscope to show.

data.prompt: What does it mean for a nucleus to be stable?

options.label: It is likely to change
options.note: That describes an unstable nucleus.

options.label: It has no protons
options.note: Every nucleus has protons.

data.explanation: A stable nucleus stays the same. An unstable nucleus can change.

data.statement: If you change the number of protons in an atom, it becomes a different element.
data.explanation: True. The number of protons tells you the element, so changing it changes the element.

data.prompt: Which of these atoms is unstable?

options.label: Carbon-12
options.note: Carbon-12 is stable.

options.label: Oxygen-16
options.note: Oxygen-16 is stable.

data.explanation: Carbon-14 is unstable, which means radioactive.

data.statement: A glass of water is made of atoms.
data.explanation: True. Water is matter, and all matter is made of atoms.

data.prompt: Look at a group of unstable nuclei. Could you tell in advance which one will change next?

options.label: No: it is random for each nucleus
Yes: the one at the front always goes first
options.note: Position does not matter. Each unstable nucleus has the same chance.

options.label: Yes: the oldest one goes first
options.note: A nucleus does not get older or due. It has the same chance every time.

data.explanation: No. When one particular nucleus changes cannot be predicted. Each unstable nucleus has the same chance, so you cannot call the next one.

data.prompt: Why can a radioactive nucleus change even when nobody does anything to it?

options.label: It is unstable, so it can change on its own
Someone must trigger it
options.note: Nobody has to trigger it. Unstable nuclei change by themselves.

options.label: It needs heat first
options.note: Heating and cooling hardly affect radioactive decay.

options.label: It is being used up
options.note: Nothing is used up. The nucleus changes into another nucleus.

data.explanation: An unstable nucleus can change on its own. That is what radioactive means.

data.prompt: The nucleus that decays is the ___.
data.explanation: The nucleus that decays is the parent. The nucleus it becomes is the daughter.

data.prompt: Which nucleus can change by itself? Tap it.
data.explanation: Carbon-14 is unstable, so it can change by itself. Carbon-12 and oxygen-16 are stable and stay as they are.

data.prompt: Match each name to what it means.

pairs.right: What comes out when it changes

data.explanation: The parent is the nucleus that decays. The daughter is the nucleus it becomes. Radiation is what comes out.

data.prompt: An unstable nucleus is left alone for a very long time. What happens?

options.label: It stays the same for ever

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. The answer comes later in the lesson.

data.statement: You can say how likely a nucleus is to change, but not exactly when it will.
data.explanation: True. An unstable nucleus has a chance of changing, but when one particular nucleus changes cannot be predicted.

data.statement: A radioactive atom needs a person to make it decay.
data.explanation: Myth. Nobody has to make an unstable nucleus change. It changes by itself.

data.prompt: Which kind of radiation is made of 2 protons and 2 neutrons?

options.label: Beta
options.note: A beta particle is a fast electron.

options.label: Gamma
options.note: Gamma is electromagnetic radiation. It is not made of protons and neutrons.

data.explanation: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons stuck together, the nucleus of a helium atom.

data.prompt: A fast electron is released from a nucleus. What is this radiation called?

options.label: Alpha
options.note: Alpha is 2 protons and 2 neutrons, not an electron.

options.label: Gamma
options.note: Gamma is electromagnetic radiation, not a particle.

data.explanation: A fast electron released from a nucleus is a beta particle.

data.prompt: A gamma ray leaves a nucleus. Does the nucleus turn into a different element?

options.label: No: a gamma ray is not a particle, so no protons leave
Yes: it loses protons
options.note: Gamma is electromagnetic radiation. No protons or neutrons leave.

options.label: Yes: every decay changes the element
options.note: Gamma carries energy away and does not change the number of protons.

data.explanation: No. Gamma is electromagnetic radiation, not a particle, so no protons or neutrons leave. The nucleus stays the same element.

data.prompt: Match each kind of radiation to what it is.
data.explanation: Alpha is 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Beta is a fast electron. Gamma is high-energy electromagnetic radiation.

data.prompt: When a radioactive nucleus changes, what can it release?
data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. The answer comes later in the lesson.

data.prompt: Is it a particle, or electromagnetic radiation? Sort each one.
data.explanation: Alpha and beta are particles. Gamma and visible light are electromagnetic radiation, and gamma carries far more energy.

data.statement: Visible light is electromagnetic radiation, just like gamma rays.
data.explanation: True. Light and gamma rays are both electromagnetic radiation. Gamma rays carry far more energy.

data.statement: Gamma radiation is made of tiny pieces of the nucleus.
data.explanation: Myth. Gamma is electromagnetic radiation, like light but far more energetic. It is not made of pieces of the nucleus.

data.statement: Alpha, beta and gamma are three versions of the same thing.
data.explanation: Myth. Alpha and beta are different particles, and gamma is electromagnetic radiation, not a particle. They are three different things.

data.prompt: Which statement about half-life is true?

options.label: It describes how a group of nuclei decreases over time
It is a timer that runs inside each atom
options.note: Half-life describes a group, not a timer in each atom.

options.label: After one half-life the radioactivity is completely gone
options.note: About half of the nuclei are still unstable.

options.label: A radioactive material stays radioactive for ever
options.note: Each radioactive material fades. Some do it fast and some very slowly.

data.explanation: Half-life describes how quickly a group of radioactive nuclei decreases. It is not a timer in each atom, and the radioactivity fades without being gone after one half-life.

data.prompt: A sample starts with 80 nuclei. After two half-lives, about how many have not changed?

options.label: About 10
options.note: Two half-lives is two halvings: 80, 40, 20.

options.label: About 40
options.note: About 40 are left after one half-life, not two.

options.label: About 60
options.note: That is far more than half of 80 after even one half-life.

data.explanation: 80 becomes about 40 after one half-life and about 20 after two.

data.prompt: A sample has gone through one half-life. Which statement is true?

options.label: About half of the nuclei have decayed, and the rest were not cut in half
Every nucleus has lost half of itself
options.note: Nuclei are not cut in half. About half of them have decayed and the others have not changed.

options.label: Every nucleus is now half as radioactive
options.note: Each nucleus is either still unstable or has already changed.

data.explanation: About half of the nuclei have decayed. The rest were not cut in half.

data.prompt: What does half-life mean?

options.label: The time for about half of a large group of nuclei to decay
The time for one atom to decay
options.note: Half-life describes a group, not one atom.

options.label: The time for each atom to lose half of itself
options.note: Atoms are not cut in half. About half of the nuclei have decayed.

options.label: The time until the sample is no longer radioactive
options.note: Some radioactivity is still there after one half-life.

data.explanation: Half-life is the time for about half of a large group of radioactive nuclei to decay.

data.prompt: The pattern is 100, 50, 25, and then about ___.
data.explanation: Each half-life takes about half of what is left. Half of 25 is about 12.

data.prompt: Start with 100 nuclei. Match the number of half-lives to about how many are left.
data.explanation: Each half-life takes about half of what is left: about 50, then about 25, then about 12.

data.prompt: There are 100 radioactive nuclei. After one half-life, what happens?

options.label: Every atom becomes half as radioactive
About half of the nuclei have decayed

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. The answer comes later in the lesson.

data.statement: In a large group of nuclei, you can predict that about half will change in one half-life.
data.explanation: True. One nucleus is unpredictable, but a large group follows a pattern.

data.statement: After one half-life, the radioactivity is gone.
data.explanation: Myth. After one half-life, about half of the nuclei are still unstable. 100 becomes about 50, then about 25, and so on. It fades, but it is not gone after one half-life.

data.statement: A radioactive atom always waits exactly one half-life before it decays.
data.explanation: Myth. Half-life describes a group, not a timer in each atom. One nucleus might change soon or much later. Only the group follows the pattern.

data.prompt: A sample has a nucleus whose daughter is also unstable. After the first decay, is the sample finished changing?

options.label: No: the daughter can decay too
Yes: a decay always ends in a stable nucleus
options.note: The daughter is unstable, so it can decay again.

options.label: Yes: the atom has disappeared
options.note: Nothing vanishes. The nucleus changed into another nucleus.

data.explanation: No. The daughter is unstable, so the sample can keep changing along the chain.

data.prompt: A chain goes Parent, then Daughter. What comes next if the daughter is unstable?

options.label: Always a stable nucleus
options.note: The next nucleus can be unstable too. The chain only ends at a stable one.

options.label: The parent again
options.note: A decay does not run backwards.

data.explanation: An unstable daughter decays again into the next generation. The chain goes on until a stable nucleus is reached.

data.prompt: Put the chain in order, from the start to the end.
data.explanation: A chain starts with the parent, goes through the daughter and the next generation, and ends at a stable nucleus.

data.prompt: A nucleus decays into a daughter. Is the daughter always stable?

options.label: No, sometimes it can be unstable too

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. The answer comes later in the lesson.

data.statement: When a nucleus decays, it changes into a different nucleus.
data.explanation: True. The parent changes into a daughter, which is a different nucleus.

data.statement: Every radioactive decay immediately creates a stable atom.
data.explanation: Myth. The daughter can be unstable too, and then it decays again. A chain only ends at a stable nucleus.

data.statement: Radioactive decay means the atom just disappears.
data.explanation: Myth. The nucleus changes into a different nucleus. Nothing simply vanishes.

data.prompt: If something is radioactive, is it automatically dangerous?

options.label: Yes: anything radioactive is dangerous
options.note: Bananas and your body are radioactive. It depends on the type, the amount and how it reaches the body.

options.label: No: radioactive things are always harmless
options.note: Some radioactive things can be harmful. It depends.

data.explanation: Radioactive does not automatically mean dangerous. It depends on the type of radiation, the amount and how it reaches the body.

data.prompt: What helps decide whether radiation matters?

options.label: The type, the amount and how it reaches the body
Only whether the material is radioactive
options.note: That is not enough. It depends on more than that.

options.label: Only how old the material is
options.note: Age alone does not decide it.

data.explanation: The type of radiation, how much there is and how it reaches the body all matter. Radioactive alone does not tell you.

data.prompt: Where does radon come from?

options.label: From radioactive materials in the ground
Only from nuclear power plants
options.note: Radon is made naturally in the ground. It is in the air everywhere.

options.label: From a gas that people make and sell
options.note: Radon is natural. It comes from decay in rocks and soil.

data.explanation: Radioactive materials in the ground, such as uranium and thorium, produce radon. It is natural.

data.prompt: Which of these arrives on Earth from space?

options.label: Radon gas
options.note: Radon comes from the ground.

options.label: Potassium-40 in food
options.note: Potassium-40 is in food and in the body.

data.explanation: Cosmic radiation arrives from space all the time.

data.prompt: Put these in order, from first to last.

items.label: Radioactive materials are in the ground
Becquerel notices a fogged photographic plate
People learn to make radioactive materials

data.explanation: Radioactivity was in nature first. Becquerel found it in 1896, and only later did people learn to make radioactive materials.

data.prompt: Which of these can have radioactive material in it?
data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. The answer comes later in the lesson.

data.prompt: Which kind is it? Natural radioactivity, cosmic radiation, or made by people? Sort each one.
data.explanation: A banana, a rock and your body hold natural radioactivity. High up, an airplane gets more cosmic radiation. Reactors and hospital sources are made by people. Radiation is part of the world, not only inside nuclear facilities.

data.statement: Radioactive materials are only found in nuclear facilities.
data.explanation: Myth. Radioactive materials are in rocks, soil, air, food and your own body. Nuclear facilities are only one place.

data.prompt: A banana holds a little radioactive potassium. What does that tell you?

options.label: Radioactive does not automatically mean dangerous
Bananas are a nuclear hazard
options.note: A tiny natural amount is normal.

options.label: Bananas were made by people
options.note: Potassium-40 is natural.

data.explanation: Bananas are a little radioactive, and that is normal. Radioactive does not automatically mean dangerous.

data.prompt: What ends a decay chain?

options.label: The first decay
options.note: A daughter can be unstable and decay again.

options.label: The radiation running out
options.note: The chain ends only when the nucleus is stable.

data.explanation: A decay chain ends when a stable nucleus is reached.

data.prompt: A nucleus decays into a new nucleus. What is the new nucleus called?

options.label: The parent
options.note: The parent is the nucleus that decays.

options.label: The radiation
options.note: Radiation is what comes out, not the new nucleus.

data.explanation: The new nucleus is the daughter. The one that decayed is the parent.

data.prompt: A burst of high-energy electromagnetic radiation leaves a nucleus. What is it?

options.label: Alpha
options.note: Alpha is a particle of 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

options.label: Beta
options.note: Beta is a fast electron.

data.explanation: High-energy electromagnetic radiation from a nucleus is gamma radiation.

data.prompt: A sequence of decays in which one nucleus changes into another is called a decay ___.
data.explanation: It is called a decay chain.

data.prompt: The parent decays, and the nucleus it becomes is the ___.
data.explanation: The nucleus that decays is the parent, and the nucleus it becomes is the daughter.

data.prompt: Half-life is the time for about ___ of a large group of nuclei to decay.
data.explanation: Half-life is the time for about half of a large group of radioactive nuclei to decay.

data.prompt: Which describes half-life best?

options.label: The time for a group to fall to about half
The time one atom takes to be cut in half
options.note: Atoms are not cut in half.

options.label: The time until nothing is radioactive
options.note: Some radioactivity is left after one half-life.

data.explanation: Half-life is the time it takes for a group of radioactive nuclei to fall to about half.

data.prompt: Which kind of radiation is the same as the nucleus of a helium atom?

options.label: Beta
options.note: Beta is a fast electron.

options.label: Gamma
options.note: Gamma is electromagnetic radiation.

data.explanation: An alpha particle, 2 protons and 2 neutrons, is the nucleus of a helium atom.

data.prompt: A sample has 100 nuclei. After one half-life, about how many have not yet changed?

options.label: About 25
options.note: That would be after two half-lives.

options.label: About 90
options.note: That is too few to have changed.

data.explanation: After one half-life, about half of the 100 nuclei are left: about 50.

data.prompt: Which of these is a natural source of radioactivity?

options.label: A radioactive source made in a reactor
options.note: That one is made by people.

options.label: Nothing: it only comes from nuclear plants
options.note: Radioactivity is in rocks, air, food, bodies and space.

data.explanation: Potassium-40 is a natural radioactive material found in food and in the body.

data.prompt: Which of these is not a particle?

options.label: An alpha particle
options.note: Alpha is a particle.

options.label: A beta particle
options.note: Beta is a particle.

data.explanation: Gamma radiation is electromagnetic radiation, not a particle.

data.prompt: A rock contains unstable nuclei. Nobody touches it. What happens to those nuclei?

options.label: Some change on their own, now and then
Nothing: they wait for someone to trigger them
options.note: Unstable nuclei do not need a trigger.

options.label: They all change at the same moment
options.note: Each nucleus changes at its own random moment.

data.explanation: Unstable nuclei change by themselves. Some change now and then, and nobody can say which one is next.

data.statement: After a decay there is still a nucleus. It is a different one.
data.explanation: True. A decay changes a nucleus into a different nucleus.

data.prompt: After three half-lives, about how much of the original group is left?

options.label: About a half
options.note: That is after one half-life.

options.label: About a quarter
options.note: That is after two half-lives.

options.label: None of it
options.note: It keeps halving but is not gone.

data.explanation: Each half-life halves what is left: a half, then a quarter, then about an eighth.

data.statement: An unstable nucleus changes by itself, without anyone starting it.
data.explanation: True. Radioactive decay is spontaneous: nobody has to trigger it.

data.statement: Anything radioactive is automatically dangerous.
data.explanation: Myth. It depends on the type of radiation, the amount and how it reaches the body.

data.statement: If you watch one unstable nucleus closely, you can tell the exact second it will change.
data.explanation: Myth. When one particular nucleus changes cannot be predicted.

data.statement: Half-life tells you exactly when one particular nucleus will decay.
data.explanation: Myth. Half-life describes a group. It cannot tell you when one nucleus will decay.

data.statement: Alpha and beta are particles.
data.explanation: True. Alpha is 2 protons and 2 neutrons and beta is a fast electron. Gamma is the one that is not a particle.

data.statement: Radon is a radioactive gas that comes from the ground.
data.explanation: True. Radioactive materials in the ground produce radon, a natural radioactive gas.

data.prompt: In a sample, one nucleus changed today. What can you say about another unstable nucleus in the same sample?

options.label: It could change today, tomorrow or much later: you cannot tell
It will change tomorrow
options.note: Nothing fixes the moment for one nucleus.

options.label: It changes at the same moment as the first
options.note: Each nucleus changes at its own random moment.

data.explanation: You cannot say when another particular nucleus will change. Only a large group follows a pattern.

data.prompt: A nucleus decays. What has happened to it?

options.label: It has changed into a different nucleus
It has vanished
options.note: Nothing simply vanishes.

options.label: It has been cut in half
options.note: A decay does not cut a nucleus in half.

data.explanation: The nucleus changed into a different nucleus. Nothing simply vanishes.

data.prompt: Why can half-life describe a group but not one nucleus?

options.label: Each nucleus changes at a random moment, but a big group follows a pattern
Each nucleus has its own timer that is set to one half-life
options.note: Half-life is not a timer in each atom.

options.label: A group has fewer nuclei, so it is easier to predict
options.note: A larger group follows the pattern better, not a smaller one.

data.explanation: One nucleus is random, but a large group follows a pattern. That pattern is what half-life describes.
